P0600.d: P0600 means a serial data link that the module relies on has failed. At Ford it is the internal link between the main processor and the monitoring processor ('quizzer') of the electronic throttle safety concept: if data cannot be exchanged or check bytes are invalid, the code sets within about a second (diesel: 5 s), usually with the check engine and wrench lamps and a throttle failure mode such as an RPM limit.
s: Check engine light, at Ford also the wrench lamp
Reduced power or RPM limit (throttle failure mode)
Harsh shifts or transmission limp mode where the line links engine and gearbox
Other monitors such as the catalyst monitor do not run
c: Internal module fault in the processor-to-processor link
Open or short in a dedicated serial line between engine and transmission module (e.g. Subaru)
Low voltage, voltage dips or a poor ground or supply at the module
Fault in the transmission module at the other end of the line

P0601.d: The module continuously calculates a checksum over its program and calibration memory (flash) and compares it with the stored value; on newer units the flash error correction also reports bit errors it cannot repair. A mismatch means the stored software is corrupted.
s: Check engine light on
Often no change in driving
Possibly no start or limp mode if the software is badly damaged
Transmission limp mode if the transmission module is affected
c: Defective flash memory in the module
Low voltage, voltage dips or a poor ground or supply at the module

P0602.d: P0602 reports that the module is not, or not completely, programmed for this vehicle. GM checks at power-up and then every second whether a service replacement module still carries no calibration, and sets the code in the first trip; in brake modules a missing calibration set or a sensor ID that does not match also counts.
s: Check engine light or service lamp
Engine may not start or runs in limp mode
Reduced engine power
Appears right after a module replacement or software update
c: Programming interrupted by a voltage dip or lost connection
Wrong or incompatible software, calibration or configuration block
Internal memory defect in the module

P0603.d: Keep alive memory holds learned values – fuel trim, idle and shift adaptation, readiness status – while the engine is off, as long as the module has constant battery power; CARB defines it as memory that is lost when the battery or fuse is disconnected. The module stores a checksum of this memory at shutdown and compares it at the next start (Ford, GM Europe); GM calls the check 'long term memory reset', and the Ford
s: Check engine light on (depending on the maker)
Rough idle or changed shifting until values are relearned
Readiness monitors reset
Often right after battery work
c: Battery disconnected, deeply discharged or replaced
Interrupted constant power feed to the module (fuse, wire, corrosion)
Main relay drops out too early, memory not saved completely at shutdown

P0604.d: P0604 means the module's working memory (RAM) failed its self-test: a value written to a cell does not read back correctly, a built-in hardware test fails, error correction reports faults, or protected memory is written without permission. GM's engine module scans the whole RAM within 30 s of start-up and then keeps checking in the background, setting the code after repeated failures with the lamp in the first trip;
s: Check engine light on
Limp mode or transmission limp mode
Intermittent stalling or starting problems
Several module codes at the same time
c: Internal hardware defect of the module (RAM)
Low voltage, voltage dips or a poor ground or supply at the module
Moisture or corrosion in the module or at its connector

P0605.d: P0605 reports an error in the module's program memory (ROM, today flash), found by a checksum or error-correction check at start-up or in the background. Ford is the main user: its engine and transmission modules compare a ROM checksum and set P0605 with the check engine light; the diesel transmission module tests once per trip at start.
s: Check engine light on
Possibly starting problems
Transmission limp mode if the transmission module is affected
Reduced power (GM Europe assignment)
c: Program memory corrupted by an interrupted reflash
Low voltage, voltage dips or a poor ground or supply at the module

P0606.d: P0606 means the module doubts the integrity of its own processor. Checks include a question-and-answer game between main and monitoring processor (GM: new seed via SPI within 450 ms; Ford: 'quizzer' level 3), arithmetic unit and register tests, stack overflow, the order in which safety-critical software runs, and the internal voltage supply (Ford diesel: 5 V rail outside 4.7–5.3 V).
s: Check engine light, at Ford also the wrench lamp
Limp mode with reduced power or RPM limit
Poor throttle response
Rarely stalling or no start
Often together with voltage codes P0562/P0563
c: Low voltage, voltage dips or a poor ground or supply at the module
Internal hardware defect (processor, voltage regulator, output stage chip)
Short on a 5 V sensor reference loading the internal supply

P0607.d: P0607 is the general 'module not working correctly' code, used when no specific memory or processor part is named. Ford sets it for wrong instruction execution or too many processor resets in engine and transmission modules; the Ford diesel after five communication errors with its monitoring chip within 20 s (a complete loss of that link is P0600).
s: Check engine light on
Limp mode or reduced power
Brief stumbling or stalling (module reset)
Several implausible codes at once
c: Internal module defect (processor, clock, monitoring chip)
Low voltage, voltage dips or a poor ground or supply at the module
Electrical interference, e.g. from a faulty alternator or ignition

P0608.d: Many engine or powertrain modules turn the raw wheel or output-shaft speed into a cleaned-up vehicle speed signal and pass it on through their own driver – a square-wave signal whose frequency rises with speed – to the instrument cluster, cruise control, radio or steering. P0608 concerns output A: the module compares the commanded driver state with the actual line state and reports a short to ground or voltage, an op
s: Speedometer dead or jumping
Cruise control not working
Odometer stops counting
Speed-dependent functions (steering, radio volume) disturbed
c: Short or open in the output line A to the receiving module
Corroded or spread connector pins at the module or receiver
Faulty receiving module pulling the line to ground
Internal driver fault in the module

P0609.d: Many engine or powertrain modules turn the raw wheel or output-shaft speed into a cleaned-up vehicle speed signal and pass it on through their own driver – a square-wave signal whose frequency rises with speed – to the instrument cluster, cruise control, radio or steering. P0609 concerns output B: the module compares the commanded driver state with the actual line state and reports a short to ground or voltage, an op
s: Speed-dependent function of the receiver on output B disturbed
Cruise control or add-on device without speed signal
Often no noticeable driving symptom
c: Short or open in the output line B to the receiving module
Corroded or spread connector pins at the module or receiver
Faulty receiving module pulling the line to ground
Internal driver fault in the module

P060A.d: Electronic throttle systems use three levels: level 1 runs the engine, level 2 recalculates key values independently on the same processor, and level 3 is a separate monitoring processor that quizzes the main one and can shut down the throttle outputs. P060A means this monitoring processor (level 3) or its cooperation with the main processor is faulty: the question-and-answer game fails, an operating system call ends
s: Check engine light, at Ford also the wrench lamp
Reduced power or limp mode
Often no driving symptoms
Rarely stalling or starting problems
c: Unstable supply voltage or poor ground at the module (weak battery, voltage spikes)
Moisture or corrosion in the module or connector

P060B.d: The analog-to-digital converter turns every analog sensor voltage into a number, so a faulty converter can falsify many values at once. The module checks it by timing its start-up calibration (GM 6.6 L diesel: 0.30 s or longer is a fault), by converting fixed internal reference voltages (about 4.73–4.83 V must be read), by grounding a test channel that must then read near 0 V (Ford diesel: over 249 mV is a fault) and
s: Check engine light, at Ford also the wrench lamp
Reduced power or limp mode
Several sensor or misfire codes at the same time
ABS/ESC warning if the brake module set the code
c: Unstable supply voltage or poor ground at the module (weak battery, voltage spikes)
Internal defect of the converter or its chip
Shorted sensor input pulling the converter reference

P060C.d: P060C reports a fault in the main processor that actually runs the engine, found either by the monitoring processor (Ford 'quizzer', level 3) or by duplicate storage and recalculation (GM). Typical findings are corrupted RAM or ROM data, arithmetic unit errors, memory address violations, a wrong program sequence or internal supply or temperature out of range (Ford diesel: internal voltage outside 1.3–3.3 V, 5 s).
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power or limp mode
Driver assistance such as adaptive cruise unavailable
Rarely stalling or no start
Transmission limp mode if the transmission module is affected
c: Unstable supply voltage or poor ground at the module (weak battery, voltage spikes)
Overheating or moisture in the module

P060D.d: The accelerator pedal has two sensor tracks. With P060D the module's own cross-check of the pedal value fails: two processors (GM: main and 'motor' processor) calculate pedal position independently and must agree, and an active test briefly pulls one track to ground – the other must not follow, otherwise the tracks are shorted together.
s: Reduced power, engine barely responds to the pedal
Check engine light or wrench lamp
Cruise control disabled
Raised idle or limp mode
c: Short between the two pedal sensor signal lines or moisture in the pedal connector

P060E.d: P060E is the throttle counterpart of P060D. The throttle body also has two position sensor tracks, and the module checks whether it can still detect a short between them: during an active test one track is influenced briefly, and the second processor (GM 'motor processor') confirms that the test actually ran.
s: Reduced power
Check engine light (GM) or service lamp (GM Europe)
Hesitant or jerky throttle response
Cruise control not working
c: Short between the throttle sensor signal lines or moisture in the throttle connector
Internal module fault (test circuit, second processor)

P060F.d: Coolant temperature feeds the torque model of the engine (friction, cold start), which the level 2 monitoring of the electronic throttle concept recalculates. P060F means the module's internal cross-check of this value failed: the temperature used by the main software and the value captured or recalculated by the monitoring level or a second converter path do not agree.
s: Check engine light or service lamp
Possibly reduced power
Radiator fan runs constantly (substitute value)
Implausible temperature gauge
c: Internal module fault in a converter or processor path
Loose contact at the coolant temperature sensor that jumps between samples
Unstable supply voltage or poor ground at the module (weak battery, voltage spikes)

P0610.d: The module checks its vehicle-specific configuration for completeness and validity: at Ford the vehicle identification block or as-built data with tyre circumference, axle ratio, transmission and options; at GM the programmed vehicle options. Ford 2012 sets P0610 when one or more fields of that block are configured wrongly, the Ford diesel checks continuously within 0.5 s; GM and Saab V6 engines set it in the first t
s: Check engine light (depending on maker and variant)
Wrong speedometer reading or shift points
Optional functions such as cruise control missing
c: Module not or wrongly configured after replacement (used part, missing as-built data)
Changed tyre size or axle ratio without updating the data
Internal memory fault of the module

P0611.d: P0611 concerns systems with a separate injector control module or injector driver stage. On GM's 6.6 L Duramax LB7/LLY the injector driver unit reports a microcontroller, monitoring or converter fault or a timeout to the engine module over CAN; the code sets after 30 of 50 checks at 125 ms with battery voltage of 10–18 V, and the lamp follows after two trips.
s: Hard or no start, especially when cold
Rough running, misfires
Lack of power
Check engine light (GM after two trips)
c: Faulty voltage converter or driver stage in the injector module (Ford 6.0 L)
Low battery voltage, weak batteries or poor ground
CAN or supply line between engine and injector module disturbed

P0612.d: Some diesels have a separate injector driver module that is powered through a relay switched by the engine module – GM's 6.6 L Duramax LB7/LLY with its injector driver unit, Ford's 6.0 L Power Stroke with its injector control module. P0612 means the commanded relay state and the voltage measured back at the output do not match.
s: Engine does not start or stalls while driving
Check engine light (GM after two trips)
Battery drain if the relay does not drop out
Often together with P0611 or injector codes
c: Injector module relay faulty (coil open, contacts welded)
Relay control or feedback wire open or corroded, fuse
Low battery voltage or ground problems
Driver in the engine module faulty

P0613.d: P0613 reports an internal processor or calculation fault in the transmission control module. It is usually set by the transmission module itself – the scan tool shows which module stored it; on some architectures the engine module reports it on the transmission module's behalf.
s: Check engine light or transmission warning
Transmission limp mode (fixed gear, harsh shifts)
Implausible shifting
Often no noticeable symptoms (sporadic false report)
c: Voltage dip, poor ground or supply at the transmission module

P0614.d: P0614 means the software or calibration variant of the engine module does not match the fitted transmission module or transmission type, or the transmission module is not registered. CARB allows modules with several calibration variants (for example manual and automatic) to share one calibration ID only if a wrong variant turns on the lamp – exactly this check.
s: Check engine light on
Possibly transmission limp mode or limited shifting
Sometimes no other symptoms
c: Engine or transmission module replaced and not matched or registered
Used module with the wrong variant (different gearbox or engine)
Software update on only one of the two modules

P0615.d: The engine module switches the starter relay coil through its own driver – GM petrol engines with 12 V stop-start use a low-side driver, the Saab 9-4X switches 12 V to the coil. CARB requires output components to be checked for open and short circuits.
s: Engine does not crank
Stop-start not working
Intermittent starting problems
Check engine light only with some makers
c: Control wire open, harness chafed or pinched, connector corroded
Relay ground, fuse or supply faulty
Driver in the engine module faulty

P0616.d: The engine module switches the starter relay coil through its own driver – GM petrol engines with 12 V stop-start use a low-side driver, the Saab 9-4X switches 12 V to the coil. CARB requires output components to be checked for open and short circuits.
s: Engine does not crank
Stop-start disabled
Possibly blown fuse in the relay circuit
Check engine light only with some makers
c: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion in the relay or fuse box
Driver in the engine module faulty

P0617.d: The engine module switches the starter relay coil through its own driver – GM petrol engines with 12 V stop-start use a low-side driver, the Saab 9-4X switches 12 V to the coil. CARB requires output components to be checked for open and short circuits.
s: Engine does not crank, or the starter keeps running
Stop-start not working
Battery drained
Check engine light only with some makers
c: Control wire shorted to a battery feed (harness damage)
Relay faulty internally (contact to coil, welded)
Voltage fed in by retrofitted electrics (remote start, alarm)
Driver in the engine module faulty

P0618.d: CARB treats gas-fuelled vehicles (CNG, LPG, also the gas mode of bi-fuel cars) like petrol cars up to model year 2018 and under an approved manufacturer plan afterwards. P0618 is meant for vehicles with a separate control module for the alternative fuel: it reports an error in that module's keep alive memory, which holds learned values while the ignition is off and loses them when power is cut – the gas counterpart o
s: Check engine or gas system warning light
Switch to petrol, gas mode blocked (bi-fuel)
Rough idle until values are relearned
Often no symptoms
c: Power interruption at the gas module (battery disconnected, fuse, loose contact)
Poor supply, ground or corrosion at the module (underbody mounting)
Software or programming fault of the gas module

P0619.d: CARB treats gas-fuelled vehicles (CNG, LPG, also the gas mode of bi-fuel cars) like petrol cars up to model year 2018 and under an approved manufacturer plan afterwards. P0619 means the separate alternative fuel module reports an error in its working memory (RAM, read/write test) or program memory (ROM/flash, checksum) – one code for both, while the engine module uses P0604 and P0605.
s: Check engine or gas system warning light
No gas operation, switch to petrol
Starting problems on dedicated gas engines
Possibly communication code U0108
c: Interrupted or faulty programming of the gas module
Voltage dips, supply, ground or corrosion

P061A.d: Electronic throttle systems run a second, independent calculation on the same processor (level 2, at Ford 'IPC – independent plausibility check') that recomputes driver demand, permitted and actual torque and their inputs, and compares them with the main software. P061A is the result of the torque comparison: the commanded or estimated torque exceeds the permitted torque for the current operating point (Ford diesel 2
s: Reduced power or limp mode, poor throttle response
Wrench, service or check engine lamp depending on the maker
Cruise control disabled
Rarely the engine shuts off
c: Engine module software or calibration fault (update available)
Contradictory inputs (pedal, throttle, air mass, cruise request) produce an implausible torque demand
Voltage dips, poor ground or supply at the module
Internal defect of the engine module
Unapproved power upgrade (torque model no longer fits)

P061B.d: Electronic throttle systems run a second, independent calculation on the same processor (level 2, at Ford 'IPC – independent plausibility check') that recomputes driver demand, permitted and actual torque and their inputs, and compares them with the main software. P061B means the torque calculation itself is inconsistent: main software and monitoring compute the torque differently.
s: Check engine light and wrench lamp
Reduced power or limp mode
Fluctuating idle (Ford petrol with dirty throttle)
Sometimes only the lamp
c: Engine module software or calibration fault (update available)
Dirty throttle or air path, idle adaptation at its limit (petrol)
Voltage dips, poor ground or supply at the module
Injector quantity deviation pushing the zero-fuel calibration out of range (diesel)
Internal defect of the engine module

P061C.d: Electronic throttle systems run a second, independent calculation on the same processor (level 2, at Ford 'IPC – independent plausibility check') that recomputes driver demand, permitted and actual torque and their inputs, and compares them with the main software. P061C means the two internal engine speed calculations from the crankshaft signal disagree.
s: Check engine, wrench or service lamp
Reduced power or RPM limit
Stumbling or brief misfires with a disturbed signal
Rarely stalling
c: Engine module software or calibration fault (update available)
Disturbed crankshaft signal (sensor, reluctor, shielding, connector, interference)
Voltage dips, poor ground or supply at the module
Internal defect of the engine module

P061D.d: Electronic throttle systems run a second, independent calculation on the same processor (level 2, at Ford 'IPC – independent plausibility check') that recomputes driver demand, permitted and actual torque and their inputs, and compares them with the main software. P061D means the independent recalculation of air mass or engine load disagrees with the main software's value.
s: Check engine and wrench lamp (Ford) or service lamp
Reduced power, poor throttle response
Often air flow or mixture codes as well
c: Implausible air mass or load signal (dirty MAF, vacuum leak after the sensor)
Engine module software or calibration fault (update available)
Dirty throttle, adaptation at its limit
Voltage dips, poor ground or supply at the module
Internal defect of the engine module

P061E.d: Electronic throttle systems run a second, independent calculation on the same processor (level 2, at Ford 'IPC – independent plausibility check') that recomputes driver demand, permitted and actual torque and their inputs, and compares them with the main software. Torque monitoring needs a reliable brake signal: brake applied means zero driver demand, cruise is cancelled, and in pedal limp mode the engine returns to
s: Wrench lamp (Ford), no check engine light
Cruise control not working
Possibly reduced power
Stop-start possibly blocked
c: Brake light switch misadjusted or faulty (both outputs do not switch together)
Engine module software or calibration fault (update available)
Faulty brake data from the ABS module or CAN disturbance
Connector or wiring fault at the brake switch
Internal defect of the engine module

P061F.d: P061F monitors the throttle position controller inside the engine module and its communication with the main processor. At Ford the main processor sends the target throttle angle to this controller (generation 2: a 312.5 Hz duty cycle signal, 10–92 % for 0–82°), which drives the throttle motor via an H-bridge; the monitoring checks that the target is implemented and reported back correctly.
s: Wrench lamp (Ford), check engine light on generation 2
Throttle in default position, raised idle, barely any response
RPM limit
c: Internal fault in the throttle controller of the engine module
Throttle stiff, sooted or iced, controller at its limit
Engine module software or calibration fault (update available)
Throttle motor connector or wiring resistance
Voltage dips, poor ground or supply at the module

P0620.d: The alternator regulator is linked to the engine module by an L (turn-on) line, an F (field) line reporting field load as a duty cycle, or on newer cars a LIN bus. P0620 is the general control circuit code.
s: Battery warning lamp on
Battery not or incorrectly charged, starting problems
Stop-start not working
Sometimes no noticeable symptoms
c: Connector or wire between module and alternator (corrosion, break, chafing)
Alternator or regulator faulty, including its LIN interface
Battery flat or faulty, jump start or charger connected

P0621.d: The alternator regulator is linked to the engine module by an L (turn-on) line, an F (field) line reporting field load as a duty cycle, or on newer cars a LIN bus. P0621 concerns the L line: the engine module applies voltage through a high-side driver and so switches the regulator's field control on and off.
s: Battery warning lamp on
Battery not or incorrectly charged, starting problems
Raised or fluctuating idle
Starting problems after a longer drive
c: L line or alternator connector open or shorted
Ground problems between engine and body

P0622.d: The alternator regulator is linked to the engine module by an L (turn-on) line, an F (field) line reporting field load as a duty cycle, or on newer cars a LIN bus. P0622 checks the F feedback: its duty cycle equals the field on-time, from which the module calculates alternator torque and raises idle under load.
s: Battery warning lamp on
Check engine light possible on GM from model year 2023
Idle fluctuates or drops when large loads switch on
Flat battery with a real charging fault
c: F line or alternator connector open or shorted
Alternator not charging (belt, brushes), duty cycle implausible

P0623.d: P0623 concerns the control of the battery warning lamp by a module's output driver, not the alternator itself. Traditionally the regulator switches the lamp through terminal L; where a module switches it instead – GM's Saab 9-4X turns the lamp on 15 s after a charging code – it can monitor its lamp output for open or short circuits.
s: Battery lamp never lights (not even at bulb check) or stays on
Real charging faults may not be displayed
Otherwise usually no driving symptoms
c: Wire or connector to the lamp or instrument cluster

P0624.d: Despite its neighbours, P0624 has nothing to do with the alternator: it is the control circuit of the 'check fuel cap' warning lamp of the evaporative system. Ford's evaporative monitor lights such a lamp when, after refuelling, the tank cannot be pulled into vacuum – a gross leak or missing cap (P0457) – and turns it off once the cap is secured; not every vehicle has this lamp.
s: Fuel cap lamp never lights or stays on
A loose cap is no longer indicated
No driving symptoms
c: Wire or connector to the warning lamp or instrument cluster
Output driver in the engine or body module

P0625.d: The alternator regulator is linked to the engine module by an L (turn-on) line, an F (field) line reporting field load as a duty cycle, or on newer cars a LIN bus. P0625 means the F feedback is too low: with the engine running the regulator reports (almost) no field duty cycle – typically an open or grounded F line, or the alternator is not charging.
s: Battery warning lamp on
Battery not or incorrectly charged, starting problems
Raised or fluctuating idle
Check engine light on some Ford variants
c: F line open or shorted to ground, connector corroded
Regulator or alternator faulty or not charging (brushes, field winding)
Alternator B+ feed missing or high resistance

P0626.d: The alternator regulator is linked to the engine module by an L (turn-on) line, an F (field) line reporting field load as a duty cycle, or on newer cars a LIN bus. P0626 means the F feedback is too high – a duty cycle near 100 % when little or no field current is expected, typically a short to battery voltage.
s: Battery or check engine lamp (Chrysler/Ford partly with MIL)
Raised idle
Possibly overvoltage or overcharging with a regulator fault
Often no driving symptoms
c: F line shorted to battery voltage (chafing), connector
Regulator faulty (field permanently on, possibly overcharging)

P0627.d: What 'fuel pump A control circuit' means differs by maker: at GM petrol engines it is the control line from the engine module to the fuel pump relay (high-side driver), at GM's LML diesel the lift pump, at Ford petrol engines with a pump driver module the secondary circuit from that module to the pump (reported as a duty cycle on a monitor line), and at Ford's 6.7 L diesel (F-650/750) the high or low side of the pump
s: Engine does not start or stalls
Lack of power or stumbling under load
Pump not audible with ignition on
Check engine light on
c: Fuel pump relay or pump driver module faulty
Wire or connector to relay or pump open or corroded (tank, underbody)
Driver in the engine module faulty

P0628.d: What 'fuel pump A control circuit' means differs by maker: at GM petrol engines it is the control line from the engine module to the fuel pump relay (high-side driver), at GM's LML diesel the lift pump, at Ford petrol engines with a pump driver module the secondary circuit from that module to the pump (reported as a duty cycle on a monitor line), and at Ford's 6.7 L diesel (F-650/750) the high or low side of the pump
s: No start or stalling
Pump does not run
Blown fuse
Check engine light on
c: Control wire to relay or pump shorted to ground (chafing)
Pump or pump module shorted internally (Ford high side)
Driver in the engine module faulty

P0629.d: What 'fuel pump A control circuit' means differs by maker: at GM petrol engines it is the control line from the engine module to the fuel pump relay (high-side driver), at GM's LML diesel the lift pump, at Ford petrol engines with a pump driver module the secondary circuit from that module to the pump (reported as a duty cycle on a monitor line), and at Ford's 6.7 L diesel (F-650/750) the high or low side of the pump
s: Pump runs constantly or after switch-off
Battery drained
Possibly no start
Check engine light on
c: Control wire shorted to a battery feed
Relay contacts welded or relay faulty internally
Moisture in the relay or fuse box
Driver in the engine module shorted

P062A.d: P062A is a plausibility check of the fuel pump control circuit, not a plain short or open. On Ford's 2023 diesels (F-250 to F-550 and 3.0 L) the lift pump module reports its status as a duty cycle; outside 78–82 % – the expected 'good' signal – the code sets after 0.5 s.
s: Check engine light on
Lack of power or stumbling
Delayed start
Often no noticeable symptoms (software case)
c: Pump driver module faulty or reporting an error status
Contact problems or resistance in signal or supply wires

P062B.d: P062B monitors the injector driver stage inside the engine module. On direct injection engines a separate driver chip generates the boost voltage for opening the injectors and is configured by the main processor via SPI; GM checks initialisation, boost voltage (petrol: 90 V or more or 40 V or less), self-test, data download and communication, and sets the code in the first trip – while it is active, single injector c
s: Check engine light (GM in the first trip)
Stumbling, misfires, loss of power
Starting problems or stalling
Other injector codes are not reported while P062B is active (GM)
c: Short to ground on an injector high-voltage or control wire, or a faulty injector
Engine module software or calibration fault (update available)
Undervoltage or supply problem (battery, main relay)
Faulty driver chip in the engine module

P062C.d: Electronic throttle systems run a second, independent calculation on the same processor (level 2, at Ford 'IPC – independent plausibility check') that recomputes driver demand, permitted and actual torque and their inputs, and compares them with the main software. Vehicle speed feeds torque monitoring through cruise control, speed limiter and gear-dependent limits.
s: Wrench lamp (Ford), check engine light only on older Ford
Cruise control not working
Possibly reduced power
c: Engine module software or calibration fault (update available)
Disturbed vehicle or output speed signal (sensor, reluctor, ABS CAN data)
Wrong tyre size or axle ratio configured in the module
Internal defect of the engine module

P062D.d: Direct-injection injectors (petrol and common-rail diesel) need a high boost voltage generated in the module to open fast; the module then holds them with pulsed battery voltage. P062D monitors this boost voltage or the shared injector supply of bank 1.
s: Check engine light (GM in the first trip)
Misfires, rough running, stumbling
Loss of power or limp mode
Hard start or no start
c: Short in an injector high-side wire or injector collapsing the boost voltage

P062E.d: Direct-injection injectors (petrol and common-rail diesel) need a high boost voltage generated in the module to open fast; the module then holds them with pulsed battery voltage. P062E is the bank 2 counterpart of P062D for V engines with separate driver circuits per bank.
s: Check engine light on
Misfires on one side of the engine
Loss of power or limp mode
Rough idle, starting problems
c: Short in an injector wire or injector of bank 2
Engine module or driver chip faulty internally
Connector or harness under the bank 2 valve cover

P062F.d: Learned values, adaptations, counters and configuration are saved to non-volatile memory (EEPROM or flash-emulated NVM) when the module shuts down. P062F means this memory failed a check: GM and GM Europe test at start-up whether the last write at shutdown completed, GM's 6.6 L diesel checks a checksum per data block and whether sectors can be erased, Ford's diesel reports read, write or erase errors (5 s).
s: Check engine or service lamp (depending on the maker, sometimes after two trips)
Learned values lost: rough idle or harsh shifts until relearned
Often no driveability symptoms
c: Shutdown interrupted (battery disconnected, voltage dip, main relay drops out too early)
Weak battery, poor ground or supply at the module
Memory defect in the module (write cycles, ageing)

P0630.d: Since model year 2005 CARB requires exactly one module to report the VIN to a scan tool, and reprogramming the VIN must erase all emission-related diagnostic data. P0630 means the engine module holds no valid VIN or one that does not fit.
s: Check engine light (some Ford trucks without)
Scan tool shows no or a wrong VIN
Ford: wrong tyre or axle data, speedometer errors

P0631.d: P0631 is the transmission module counterpart of P0630: the transmission control module holds no VIN, an invalid one, or one that does not match the vehicle – usually compared with the VIN of the engine or body module. Typical is a replaced transmission module or mechatronic unit (on dual-clutch and automatic gearboxes with integrated control) that was not VIN-programmed, or a used part.

Scan tool shows no or a wrong VIN in the transmission module
Transmission adaptation possibly impossible
Driving often normal
c: Transmission module or mechatronic unit replaced, VIN not written

P0632.d: Engine modules increasingly keep their own copy of the odometer reading or take it over from the instrument cluster or body module; for model years 2019–2021 onward CARB requires mileage in the module's operating data records and explicitly mentions the case 'odometer is lost'. P0632 means the engine module holds no valid odometer value.

Scan tool shows no or a different mileage in the engine module
Implausible service or oil change displays
c: Engine module replaced, mileage not transferred
Several modules (engine, body, cluster) replaced or programmed at the same time
No communication to the cluster or body module during takeover

P0633.d: The immobiliser couples the engine module to the immobiliser control module (GM body module, Chrysler SKIM/WCM) through a secret key and a challenge-response exchange – 'key' here means these security data, not the ignition key. P0633 means the engine module has not learned this secret key yet.

Security or immobiliser lamp on or flashing
Code present after engine module replacement until learned
Sometimes immobiliser communication codes
c: Engine module replaced, immobiliser not learned
Learn procedure aborted or learn mode not exited (no start for another reason)
Communication fault to the immobiliser module

P0634.d: The module measures its own circuit board temperature with an internal sensor and sets P0634 when it overheats. In practice this concerns mainly transmission modules mounted in or on the gearbox, such as GM's 6T70/6T75 and 6L units with the module in the valve body, surrounded by transmission fluid.

Manual shifting disabled
Transmission warning, check engine light depending on the maker
Often together with transmission overtemperature (P0218)

Charging system overvoltage (18 V or more)
Faulty internal temperature sensor or valve body module
High sustained load (towing, mountain driving, heat)

The module compares target and actual angle and the duty cycle the motor needs; if the plate does not follow, it is de-energised and springs to its rest position, and power is limited.

P0641.d: The engine module feeds several sensors (pedal, throttle, pressure and position sensors) from shared, regulated 5 V reference circuits; 'A' is circuit 1. A short on one sensor or its wire pulls down every sensor on that circuit and triggers many follow-up codes – so look for the one faulty sensor or chafed wire, for example by unplugging the sensors one at a time.

Possibly starting or boost problems

P0644.d: P0644 concerns a dedicated serial line on which the engine module sends values or warnings to a driver display or information display – not the general vehicle CAN bus. The module reports missing or invalid communication on that line (open, short, display not answering); CARB requires digital outputs to be checked for communication faults.

Information in the driver display missing, frozen or jumping
Display stays dark

P0645.d: The engine module switches the A/C compressor clutch relay through a low-side driver once the climate control requests cooling. P0645 is the general circuit fault of the relay coil control, usually an open circuit.

Compressor runs constantly

Rarely no start if a shared fuse has blown (GM 3.4 L)

Relay or clutch supply fuse blown (e.g. shorted clutch coil)
Output driver in the module faulty

P0646.d: The engine module switches the A/C compressor clutch relay through a low-side driver once the climate control requests cooling. P0646 means the voltage at the control output is too low while the driver is off – the control wire is shorted to ground, so the relay can pull in permanently and the compressor keeps running, which can ice up the evaporator.

Evaporator ices up, cooling drops
With an open circuit: no cooling
c: Control wire between relay and module shorted to ground (chafing)
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Output driver in the module faulty

P0647.d: The engine module switches the A/C compressor clutch relay through a low-side driver once the climate control requests cooling. P0647 means the voltage at the control output stays too high while the driver switches on (it should pull to ground) – the control wire is shorted to voltage; the driver shuts off for protection and the relay does not pull in, so there is no cooling.

Compressor clutch never engages
Code stored, check engine light usually off
c: Control wire shorted to a supply wire (chafing)
Relay with internal short (coil bypassed, very low resistance)
Output driver in the module faulty

Code stored
Engine start normally not affected

Output driver in the module faulty

Output driver in the module faulty

Hard start, stumbling or lack of power from low fuel pressure

Fuel pressure codes as well (e.g. P0087)

Output stage overheating from a stiff or worn pump or poor module cooling
Supply or ground fault or corrosion at the module (often on frame or tank)

P064B.d: A power take-off (PTO) drives equipment on trucks and pick-ups – tipper, crane, hydraulic pump or winch – from the engine or transmission. A PTO control module, or the PTO function in the engine module, manages switching, working speed and release conditions; P064B reports a fault of this module or an implausible PTO request.

Engine speed hunts with PTO active or stays below about 1100 rpm (Chrysler)
Warning lamp or stored code; driving usually normal

PTO equipment installed or programmed incorrectly by the upfitter
Harness, connector or supply of the PTO module or switches

P064C.d: On diesels a glow plug control module switches the glow plugs (at Ford also the DEF heaters) with semiconductor switches, diagnoses itself and reports to the engine module. P064C means this module reports an internal fault.

Hard cold start, long cranking in cold weather
White smoke and rough running after a cold start
Glow plug circuit codes as well

Insufficient supply or ground (battery, corrosion, main fuse)
Short in a glow plug or wire overloading a driver
Moisture or corrosion in the connector of the engine-mounted module

P064D.d: Wide-band oxygen sensors need a pump current control; inside the engine module a dedicated chip (ASIC, for example Bosch's CJ125 family) regulates it, measures lambda, diagnoses sensor wiring and heater, and talks to the main processor via SPI. P064D means this chip for bank 1 sensor 1 does not work correctly or its messages are invalid.
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption, rough running (open loop)
Failed emissions test
Codes for the bank 1 sensor 1 wide-band sensor
c: Wiring or sensor fault pushing the chip into an invalid state (short to battery voltage, water in connector)

P064E.d: Wide-band oxygen sensors need a pump current control; inside the engine module a dedicated chip (ASIC, for example Bosch's CJ125 family) regulates it, measures lambda, diagnoses sensor wiring and heater, and talks to the main processor via SPI. P064E is the bank 2 counterpart of P064D and only occurs on V and boxer engines with two sensors before the catalysts.
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption, rough running
Failed emissions test
Codes for the bank 2 sensor 1 wide-band sensor
c: Wiring or connector fault of the bank 2 sensor 1

P064F.d: P064F means the module has found that its software or calibration is not the version released by the manufacturer, or fails an authenticity check (signature, checksum, security keys). CARB requires manufacturers to protect calibrations against changes without special tools and to report calibration IDs and checksums.
s: Check engine light (GM in the first trip)
Possibly follow-up codes in other modules or communication problems
Driving often normal
c: Unapproved or tuned software (chip tuning, programmer)
Faulty or interrupted reflash, outdated software
Used or replaced module without learning the security keys, wrong configuration

P0650.d: The engine module switches the check engine light (MIL) through a low-side driver – or sends the command over CAN – and monitors the circuit: with the lamp off the line must carry supply voltage, with it on nearly 0 V. CARB requires the MIL to light for a bulb check at ignition on with the engine off (at least 15 s since model year 2005).

MIL stays on (with a short or combined code)
Code only visible with a scan tool, engine runs normally
Failed emissions inspection
c: Wire or connector between engine module and instrument cluster open or corroded
MIL bulb burnt out or LED/instrument cluster faulty
MIL supply in the cluster missing (fuse, ignition feed)
Short in the circuit (at GM reported as P263A/P263B)
Output driver in the module faulty

Starting problems or stalling

A sensor signal wire shorted to voltage

Poor supply or ground of module 2

P06FB.d: P06FB means glow plug control module 2 has found a memory checksum error – the counterpart of P06DF for module 1. The module forms a checksum over its memory at power-up and compares it with the stored value.
s: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp
Hard cold start, long cranking in frost
Rough cold idle and white smoke, often one cylinder bank only
Usually no symptoms when warm

P06FC.d: P06FC means the feedback or communication from glow plug control module 2 to the engine module is missing, or the line is open or shorted – the counterpart of P0683 for module 1. Depending on design the module reports over a single feedback wire (Bosch-type systems expect it inverse to the command line) or over the bus; GM and Ford report a lost bus link as U0106 rather than P0683.
s: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp
Hard cold start, long cranking in frost
Rough cold idle and white smoke, often one cylinder bank only
Usually no symptoms when warm
c: Feedback or bus line open or shorted, connector corroded
Glow module 2 without supply (does not transmit)
Glow module 2 or engine module interface faulty

P06FD.d: P06FD means signals or messages from glow plug control module 2 arrive at the engine module but are implausible – wrong duty cycle or pattern, feedback not matching the command, or single messages timing out. It is the counterpart of P0684 for module 1; Saab's Bosch-based diesels, for example, expect the feedback signal to be inverse to the command line.
s: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp
Hard cold start, long cranking in frost
Rough cold idle and white smoke, often one cylinder bank only
Usually no symptoms when warm
c: Loose contact or contact resistance in the feedback or bus line
Ground offset between module and engine module from glow currents
Software mismatch between modules or module faulty

P06FE.d: 'Diesel intake air flow control' is the diesel's electric intake throttle with position sensor (P02E0 ff). During cold start many diesels close it partly: the extra load raises exhaust temperature so the catalysts light off sooner.
s: Check engine light, usually after two trips
Hardly any change in driveability
Possibly more smoke or smell while warming up
Further throttle codes (P02E1/P02E4/P02E5) possible
c: Intake throttle coked with soot and oil (EGR, crankcase ventilation)
Throttle motor or gear stiff, position sensor faulty
Ice or condensate in the intake in frost
Contact resistance in connector or wiring, low voltage

P06FF.d: When the engine module switches a lamp through its own wire, it checks the output driver electrically like other lamp outputs: with the lamp off the line must carry supply voltage, with it on nearly 0 V – GM's MIL driver, for example, flags an open circuit at 200 kΩ or more. It cannot see whether the bulb lights, and on cars that send the lamp command over CAN such faults appear as U codes.
s: ECO indicator not working or permanently lit
No effect on driving
c: Wire or connector to the lamp open or shorted
